title: Receiving antennas and direction finding
blurb: Explain why Beverage antennas are terminated, why low-band receiving favors directivity over loss, and how loops and sense antennas find bearings.

E9H01.why: A Beverage works on a traveling wave along the wire, so it should be **at least one wavelength long**. It runs low over ground.

E9H02.why: Low-band atmospheric noise is so high that **directivity matters more than loss**: loss cuts signal and noise together.

E9H03.why: RDF is **peak gain compared with the average gain** over the hemisphere around and above the antenna.
E9H03.trap: Front-to-back ratio and gain over a dipole are different measures.

E9H04.why: The shield blocks **unbalanced capacitive coupling** to the surroundings, so the nulls get deeper.

E9H05.why: A small loop's pattern has **two opposite nulls** (bidirectional), so a bearing is ambiguous by 180°.
E9H05.trap: Its null is sharp: that's why loops are used for direction finding.

E9H06.why: The right resistance gives the **least SWR variation** over the band: the reverse wave is absorbed instead of reflected.

E9H07.why: The resistor **absorbs signals arriving from the reverse direction** instead of letting them reflect back.

E9H08.why: A sense antenna adds an omnidirectional signal that **turns the loop's two nulls into one**.

E9H09.why: A terminated single-turn loop such as a pennant is unidirectional: a **cardioid** pattern.

E9H10.why: Output voltage grows with **turns × area enclosed**. More of either means more voltage.

E9H11.why: A cardioid has a **single null**, so the bearing isn't ambiguous by 180°.
E9H11.trap: Direction finders use nulls because they are sharper than peaks.
